steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing the Expressive Leaky Memory (ELM) neuron, a compact, biologically inspired phenomenological model of a cortical neuron. Motivate why single-neuron computation matters and why surrogate models are useful, introduce the model, summarize the experimental findings, and list the contributions.

steps.text:

- Evidence that cortical neurons are sophisticated, and the mechanisms behind it
- Biophysical models vs. phenomenological surrogate models; prior TCN result
- Our proposal: the ELM neuron
- Experimental findings
- Contributions

  - view 2: intrinsic computational power of individual neurons contributes a significant part

  - mechanisms: complex ion channel dynamics (e.g. NMDA nonlinearity), plasticity on various/longer timescales (e.g. slow spike frequency adaptation), intricate morphology (e.g. nonlinear dendritic integration), and their interactions

  - recent study: temporal convolutional network captures spike-level I/O with millisecond precision, integrating synaptic input across whole dendritic tree of high-fidelity model
  - needed highly expressive TCN with millions of parameters
- Our proposal: ELM neuron
  - hypothesis: biologically inspired components aligned with high-level computational principles -> much smaller model
  - needs multiple mechanisms of neural expressivity; allocate resources/parameters judiciously, roughly like biological neurons
  - if possible, design choices -> conceptual insight into neural computation
  - ELM: biologically inspired phenomenological model of cortical neuron (Figure 1)
  - low-level biology abstracted away for efficiency; parameters not directly biophysically interpretable
  - ablations still give conceptual insights into needed components
  - recurrent cell, drop-in replacement for LSTMs
- Findings
  - ELM variant matches spike-level I/O of detailed layer 5 pyramidal neuron model at millisecond resolution with a few thousand parameters vs. millions for TCNs
  - accurate surrogates need multiple memory-like hidden states w/ longer timescales + highly nonlinear synaptic integration

  - LRA long sequence benchmarks incl. Pathfinder-X: over 70\% accuracy, many transformer-based models don't learn at all

  - propose ELM: recurrent cell inspired by cortical neurons
  - efficiently learns I/O of biophysical cortical neuron model -> well-aligned inductive biases
  - ablations help formulate/validate hypotheses on high-level neuronal computation
  - long-sequence processing via long memory and synapse timescales

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The human brain has impressive computational capabilities, but the exact mechanisms behind them are still largely undetermined. There are two complementary directions that people pursue when looking for the mechanisms of brain computation. In one direction, many researchers study how these capabilities could come from the collective activity of neurons that are connected into a complex network structure, where the individual neurons can be as basic as leaky integrators or ReLU neurons. In the other direction, it has been proposed that the intrinsic computational power that individual neurons have contributes a significant part of the computations.

Most work focuses on the first hypothesis, but there is more and more evidence that cortical neurons are remarkably sophisticated, even comparable to expressive multilayered artificial neural networks, and that they can discriminate between dozens to hundreds of input patterns. Many biological mechanisms have been identified that contribute to this complexity, such as complex ion channel dynamics (e.g. NMDA nonlinearity), plasticity on various and especially longer timescales (e.g. slow spike frequency adaptation), the intricate cell morphology (e.g. nonlinear integration by the dendritic tree), and the interactions between them.

Detailed biophysical models of cortical neurons try to capture this complexity with high-fidelity mechanistic simulations. But they need a lot of computing resources to run, and they usually work at a very fine level of granularity, which does not help with extracting higher-level insights into the computational principles of the neuron. One promising way to get such higher-level insights from simulations is to train surrogate phenomenological neuron models. These models are designed to replicate the output of the biophysical simulations, but they use simplified interpretable components. This approach was used for example to model the computation in the dendritic tree with a simple two-layer ANN. Building on this research, a recent study developed a temporal convolutional network that captures the spike-level input/output (I/O) relationship with millisecond precision, which accounts for the complexity of integrating diverse synaptic input across the whole dendritic tree of a high-fidelity biophysical neuron model. They found that a highly expressive temporal convolutional network with millions of parameters was essential to reproduce this I/O relationship.

- Our proposal: ELM neuron
  - hypothesis: biologically inspired components aligned w/ high-level computational principles of cortical neuron -> capture I/O with much smaller model
  - needs multiple mechanisms of neural expressivity, judicious allocation of resources/parameters (rough analogy to biology)
  - if possible -> design choices give conceptual insights into neural computation
  - ELM (Figure 1): biologically inspired phenomenological cortical neuron model
  - low-level processes abstracted for efficiency; parameters not directly biophysically interpretable; ablations still informative
  - recurrent cell, drop-in replacement for LSTMs
- Findings
  - ELM variant matches spike-level I/O of layer 5 pyramidal neuron model, millisecond resolution, few thousand params (vs. millions for TCNs)
  - need: multiple memory-like hidden states, longer timescales, highly nonlinear synaptic integration
  - neuromorphic dataset (addition of spike-encoded spoken digits): beats classic LSTMs via slowly decaying memory + nonlinear integration
  - LRA benchmarks incl. Pathfinder-X: over 70\% accuracy; many transformer-based models don't learn
- Contributions
  1. propose ELM neuron, recurrent cell inspired by cortical neurons
  2. efficiently learns biophysical neuron I/O -> inductive biases well aligned
  3. ablations -> formulate/validate hypotheses about high-level neuronal computation
  4. long-sequence processing via long memory and synapse timescales

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The human brain has impressive computational capabilities, but the exact mechanisms behind them are still largely undetermined. There are two complementary directions that people pursue when looking for the mechanisms of brain computation. In one direction, many researchers study how these capabilities could come from the collective activity of neurons that are connected into a complex network structure, where the individual neurons can be as basic as leaky integrators or ReLU neurons. In the other direction, it has been proposed that the intrinsic computational power that individual neurons have contributes a significant part of the computations.

Most work focuses on the first hypothesis, but there is more and more evidence that cortical neurons are remarkably sophisticated, even comparable to expressive multilayered artificial neural networks, and that they can discriminate between dozens to hundreds of input patterns. Many biological mechanisms have been identified that contribute to this complexity, such as complex ion channel dynamics (e.g. NMDA nonlinearity), plasticity on various and especially longer timescales (e.g. slow spike frequency adaptation), the intricate cell morphology (e.g. nonlinear integration by the dendritic tree), and the interactions between them.

Detailed biophysical models of cortical neurons try to capture this complexity with high-fidelity mechanistic simulations. But they need a lot of computing resources to run, and they usually work at a very fine level of granularity, which does not help with extracting higher-level insights into the computational principles of the neuron. One promising way to get such higher-level insights from simulations is to train surrogate phenomenological neuron models. These models are designed to replicate the output of the biophysical simulations, but they use simplified interpretable components. This approach was used for example to model the computation in the dendritic tree with a simple two-layer ANN. Building on this research, a recent study developed a temporal convolutional network that captures the spike-level input/output (I/O) relationship with millisecond precision, which accounts for the complexity of integrating diverse synaptic input across the whole dendritic tree of a high-fidelity biophysical neuron model. They found that a highly expressive temporal convolutional network with millions of parameters was essential to reproduce this I/O relationship.

In this work, we propose that a model with appropriate biologically inspired components, which align with the high-level computational principles of a cortical neuron, should be able to capture the I/O relationship with a much smaller model size. For this, a model would probably need to account for multiple mechanisms of neural expressivity and allocate computational resources and parameters judiciously, roughly like biological neurons do. If such a construction is possible, the design choices it needs may give insights into the principles of neural computation at the conceptual level. We go on to design the Expressive Leaky Memory (ELM) neuron model (see Figure 1), which is a biologically inspired phenomenological model of a cortical neuron. Although it is biologically inspired, low-level biological processes are abstracted away for computational efficiency, and so the individual parameters of the ELM neuron are not designed to be directly biophysically interpretable. Still, model ablations can give conceptual insights into the computational components that are needed to emulate the cortical input/output relationship. The ELM neuron works as a recurrent cell and can be conveniently used as a drop-in replacement for LSTMs.

Our experiments show that a variant of the ELM neuron is expressive enough to accurately match the spike level I/O of a detailed biophysical model of a layer 5 pyramidal neuron at a millisecond temporal resolution, with a few thousand parameters, which is very different from the millions of parameters that temporal convolutional networks need. Conceptually, we find that accurate surrogate models need multiple memory-like hidden states with longer timescales and highly nonlinear synaptic integration. To explore what neuron-internal timescales and sophisticated synaptic integration into multiple memory units imply, we first test its temporal information integration capabilities on a challenging biologically inspired neuromorphic dataset, which requires adding spike-encoded spoken digits. We find that the ELM neuron can outperform classic LSTMs by using a sufficient number of slowly decaying memory and highly nonlinear synaptic integration. Then we evaluate the ELM neuron on the well-established LRA benchmarks for long sequence modeling from the machine learning literature, including the Pathfinder-X task which is notoriously challenging, and where it gets over 70\% accuracy while many transformer-based models do not learn at all.

Our contributions are the following.

- 1. We propose the Expressive Leaky Memory (ELM) neuron model, a phenomenological model and recurrent cell architecture inspired by biological cortical neurons.

- 2. The ELM neuron learns the input/output relationship of a sophisticated biophysical model of a cortical neuron efficiently, which indicates that its inductive biases are well aligned.

- 3. With suitable architectural ablations, the ELM neuron helps to formulate and validate hypotheses about the underlying high-level neuronal computations.

- 4. Lastly, we show that the ELM neuron has considerable long-sequence processing capabilities by using long memory and synapse timescales.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The human brain has impressive computational capabilities, yet the precise mechanisms underlying them remain largely undetermined. Two complementary directions are pursued in the search for mechanisms of brain computation. On the one hand, many researchers investigate how these capabilities could arise from the collective activity of neurons connected into a complex network structure [1,2,3], where individual neurons might be as basic as leaky integrators or ReLU neurons. On the other hand, it has been proposed that the intrinsic computational power of individual neurons [4,5,6] contributes a significant part of the computations.

Although most work focuses on the former hypothesis, increasing evidence indicates that cortical neurons are remarkably sophisticated [6,7,8], even comparable to expressive multilayered artificial neural networks [9,10,11,12], and capable of discriminating between dozens to hundreds of input patterns [13,14,15]. Numerous biological mechanisms have been identified as contributing to this complexity, such as complex ion channel dynamics (e.g. NMDA nonlinearity [16,17,18]), plasticity on various and especially longer timescales (e.g. slow spike frequency adaptation [19,20]), the intricate cell morphology (e.g. nonlinear integration by the dendritic tree [21,22,8]), and their interactions.

Detailed biophysical models of cortical neurons aim to capture this complexity through high-fidelity mechanistic simulations [23,24,25]. However, they require substantial computing resources and typically operate at a very fine level of granularity that does not facilitate extracting higher-level insights into the neuron’s computational principles. A promising approach for deriving such insights from simulations is to train surrogate phenomenological neuron models, which are designed to replicate the output of biophysical simulations using simplified interpretable components. This approach was employed, for example, to model computation in the dendritic tree via a simple two-layer ANN [9,26,27]. Building on this line of research, a recent study by [11] developed a temporal convolutional network to capture the spike-level input/output (I/O) relationship with millisecond precision, accounting for the complexity of integrating diverse synaptic input across the entire dendritic tree of a high-fidelity biophysical neuron model. It was found that a highly expressive temporal convolutional network with millions of parameters was essential to reproduce this I/O relationship.

In this work, we propose that a model equipped with appropriate biologically inspired components that align with the high-level computational principles of a cortical neuron should be able to capture the I/O relationship with a substantially smaller model size. To achieve this, a model would likely need to account for multiple mechanisms of neural expressivity and to allocate computational resources and parameters judiciously, in rough analogy to biological neurons. If such a construction is possible, the required design choices may yield insights into the principles of neural computation at the conceptual level. We therefore design the Expressive Leaky Memory (ELM) neuron model (see Figure 1), a biologically inspired phenomenological model of a cortical neuron. While biologically inspired, it abstracts away low-level biological processes for computational efficiency, and consequently its individual parameters are not designed for direct biophysical interpretability. Nevertheless, model ablations can provide conceptual insights into the computational components required to emulate the cortical input/output relationship. The ELM neuron functions as a recurrent cell and can conveniently be used as a drop-in replacement for LSTMs [28].

Our experiments show that a variant of the ELM neuron is expressive enough to accurately match the spike level I/O of a detailed biophysical model of a layer 5 pyramidal neuron at millisecond temporal resolution with a few thousand parameters, in stark contrast to the millions of parameters required by temporal convolutional networks. Conceptually, we find that accurate surrogate models require multiple memory-like hidden states with longer timescales and highly nonlinear synaptic integration. To explore the implications of neuron-internal timescales and sophisticated synaptic integration into multiple memory units, we first probe the model's temporal information integration capabilities on a challenging biologically inspired neuromorphic dataset that requires the addition of spike-encoded spoken digits. We find that the ELM neuron can outperform classic LSTMs by leveraging a sufficient number of slowly decaying memory and highly nonlinear synaptic integration. We then evaluate the ELM neuron on the well-established LRA long sequence modeling benchmarks from the machine learning literature, including the notoriously challenging Pathfinder-X task, where it achieves over 70\% accuracy while many transformer-based models do not learn at all.

Our contributions are the following.

- 1. We propose the phenomenological Expressive Leaky Memory (ELM) neuron model, a recurrent cell architecture inspired by biological cortical neurons.

- 2. The ELM neuron efficiently learns the input/output relationship of a sophisticated biophysical model of a cortical neuron, indicating that its inductive biases are well aligned.

- 3. Using suitable architectural ablations, the ELM neuron facilitates formulating and validating hypotheses about the underlying high-level neuronal computations.

- 4. Lastly, we demonstrate the considerable long-sequence processing capabilities of the ELM neuron enabled by long memory and synapse timescales.
